Uniform Title: Advayatārakopaniṣat Main Title: Yoga Upaniṣads with the Commentary of Śrī Upaniṣadbrahmayogin Secondary Title: Advayatārakā Upaniṣat
Commentator: Brahmayogin (also known as Śrī Upaniṣad-Brahmayogin) Editor: Śāstrī Mahādeva
Notes: Transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: January 29, 2007.

The Advayatārakopaniṣad. "That is full"—thus [ends] the peace invocation. The section on the yoga of the Savior (Tāraka).
Now, therefore, we shall expound the Advayatāraka Upaniṣad for the ascetic who has conquered his senses and is perfected in the six virtues beginning with tranquility (śama). || 1 ||
The Vivaraṇa composed by the Brahmayogin Upaniṣadbrahma:
Oṃ, salutations to the venerable Ramacandra, the supreme Guru and Great Swan (Paramahaṃsa) who is the substratum of the entire universe;
[salutations to] the Tāraka [mantra], which is non-dual and fully perfected through the realization that duality is impossible.
I praise the glory of Śrī Rāma, sung as the Tāraka Brahman.

Indeed, this *Advayatārakopaniṣad*, which is a division of the White Yajurveda, is seen here to reveal the entire essence of Rājayoga and to culminate in Brahman alone. A commentary on this [text], though brief in its wording, is now commenced. Here, it is said—"Now" (*atha*)—that the Śrutis teach the Tāraka-yoga for the sake of the qualified seeker as described, following the exposition of the two sections concerning ritual action (*karma-kāṇḍa*) and meditative worship (*upāsanā-kāṇḍa*), because the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is not accomplished by means of those [two].

p. 2) For that purpose, that wherein no duality exists apart from itself is the non-dual Brahman; the *Vidyā* (knowledge) that awakens one to that alone is the *Tārakopaniṣad*, which we, the Śrutis, shall now explain. To whom is this addressed? To this he says: "to the ascetics" (*yatayaḥ*). An ascetic is one who, having first performed the duties of his own stage of life (*āśrama*), has heard the Vedānta from the mouth of a teacher and then practiced reflection (*manana*) through reasonings not contradictory to the Śruti, all for the sake of meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). Why is there asceticism for one whose senses are unsubdued? To this he says: "to the one who has conquered the senses" (*jitendriyāya*). This is because asceticism is possible only for one who has conquered the senses. Why does one overcome the sixfold group of enemies (*ariṣaḍvarga*) have mastery over the senses? To this he says: "to the one perfected in the six virtues beginning with tranquility" (*śamādiṣaḍguṇapūrṇāya*). This is because the attainment of the six virtues, such as tranquility (*śama*), is preceded by the cessation of the sixfold group of enemies. Thus, the meaning is that the Śrutis instruct the *tāraka-yoga* to one who possesses such means. || 1 ||

Constantly contemplating, "I am the very nature of consciousness," which is both the means and the fruit of yoga, with eyes either fully closed or slightly opened, one beholds with an inward vision the Supreme Brahman in the form of a mass of light—Existence-Consciousness-Bliss—above the hollow of the eyebrows; thus beholding, one becomes that very form. || 2 ||

Thus he describes the means and the fruit of *nididhyāsana* (contemplation) with the word "cit" (consciousness). The yogi, contemplating within himself, "I am of the nature of consciousness," with eyes half-closed, beholding in the space between the eyebrows and other such places that which is pure Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*)—thinking "I am Brahman"—becomes of that very form, taking on the nature of the Star (the point of light). || 2 ||

It is called *tāraka* because it delivers one from the great fear of the cycle of birth, old age, death, and transmigration (*saṃsāra*). Having realized that both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) are products of *māyā*, and having discarded all distinctions through the "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), that which remains is the non-dual Brahman. || 3 ||

To the question "What is the *tāraka* (the savior)? he says: "The *garbha*... etc. The meaning is that the *tāraka* is the inner self (*pratyagātman*), because it saves one from the cycle of worldly existence—such as dwelling in the womb—which is imagined by one's own ignorance (*svājñā-vikalpita*). This is because the light-linga (*jyotir-liṅga*), established by scripture as "the ascetic should always meditate eternally on the light-linga between the eyebrows," exists in the form of the inner self. Having raised the doubt, "If there is a difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), how can there be the state of being Brahman, which is non-different from the inner self?", he says "The *jīva*... etc. (Verse 3). Since the difference between those two is illusory (*māyika*) and therefore false, he states that whatever remains after that [negation] is indeed Brahman.
The method for contemplating the three targets:
for the sake of attaining that, one must practice the contemplation of the three targets. || 4 ||
To the question of how the means for attaining that [liberation] is, he says: "by its accomplishment" (tatsiddhyā). || 4 ||
The internal characteristic of the target.

Within the body, the Brahma-nāḍī, known as Suṣumṇā, exists in the form of the sun; it is filled with the light of the full moon. Starting from the *mūlādhāra*, it extends to the aperture of Brahman (*brahmarandhra*). In its center resides the one renowned as Kuṇḍalinī, possessing a brilliance equal to ten million flashes of lightning and a body as subtle as a lotus fiber. By beholding her with the mind alone, a person becomes liberated through the destruction of all sins. If one perceives, through the continuous flashing of the yoga of the star-like light, the specific circle above the palate and the forehead, one becomes a perfected being (*siddha*). When the two ear-cavities are opened by the tips of the index fingers, a whistling sound (*phūtkāra*) arises there. With the mind fixed therein, having gazed at the spot of blue light situated between the eyes, one attains unsurpassed bliss through internal vision. One likewise perceives this within the heart. Thus, the characteristic of the internal object of focus (*antarlakṣya*) should be meditated upon by those seeking liberation. || 5 ||

The object of focus (*lakṣya*) is threefold, according to the division of internal, external, and intermediate. Regarding that, he states the definition of the internal object of focus and its fruit of practice, beginning with the word "deha" (the body): when Kuṇḍalinī, by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the gaze, the mind, and fire, [reaches] the downward-facing mouth of the Suṣumnā, which is adorned at the tip of the triangle at the Mūlādhāra.

(4) Having pierced the downward-facing mouth of the *suṣumnā*, which is adorned at its tip by a triangle, the sage’s inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) enters into its center. Then, preceded by the forgetting of the internal and external phenomenal world (*prapañca*), it attains the state of non-conceptual Brahman (*nirvikalpa-brahma-pada*). The meaning is that through non-conceptual knowledge, the sage becomes liberated from conceptualization (*vikalpa*). To the question, "What is the means for achieving that?", he says: "The *phāla* [the plow]. Stating the means for experiencing the bliss residing therein, he concludes the section on the internal *lakṣmī*: "The index finger... and so forth. One attains bliss. Not only in the two ear-cavities, but likewise in the heart. (5)
The characteristic of the external object of focus.

Now, the characteristic of the external object: if one perceives the sky at the tip of the nose—gradually extending to the end of four, six, eight, ten, or twelve finger-breadths—endowed with two colors, namely a blue luster and a shimmering redness resembling the hue of a dark cloud or a flash of yellow, then he becomes a yogī. For the person who gazes at the region of the sky with a moving gaze, rays of light appear before his vision; by seeing them, he becomes a yogī. If he sees rays of light resembling molten gold at the corners of his eyes or on the ground, his vision becomes steady. For one who gazes twelve finger-breadths above the head, immortality is attained. Wherever one may be situated, if the celestial light is seen upon the head, he indeed becomes a yogī. || 6 ||

He states the definition of the external object (*bāhyalakṣya*): "Now" (*atha*), etc. It should be understood that the entire *Upaniṣad*, beginning with "the yogin becomes," has for the most part been explained by means of the commentary on the *Maṇḍala-brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad*. || 6 ||
Now, regarding the characteristic of the middle object:

at dawn, one perceives it as being like the undivided solar disc with its various colors, like a series of flames of fire, or like the sky devoid of those [elements], by virtue of being formed in that very shape.

(p. 5) It remains [there]. Through repeated observation of that, it becomes the *guṇarahita-ākāśa* (the space devoid of qualities). It becomes the *paramākāśa* (supreme space), resembling dense darkness illuminated by the form of shimmering stars. It becomes the *mahākāśa* (great space), shining like the fire of time (*kālānala*). It becomes the *tattvākāśa* (reality-space), shining with the most excellent and supreme luster. It becomes the *sūryākāśa* (sun-space), resembling the majestic radiance of ten million suns. Thus, the fivefold space situated externally and internally has the star as its objective mark (*lakṣya*). One who perceives that attains the fruit of liberation and becomes equal to such space. Therefore, the star alone is the objective mark that bestows the fruit of the state beyond the mind (*amanaska*). || 7 ||

Having described the nature of the internal and external objects of focus, he states the nature of the intermediate object of focus with the word "atha" (now). One who perceives that [intermediate state] is liberated from one's own ignorance, its effects, and their fruits. Since this is so, therefore... || 7 ||
That *tāraka* is of two kinds: the first half is *tāraka*, and the second half is *amanaska*. Regarding this, there is this verse:
Know that yoga to be twofold according to the preceding and subsequent methods:
know the former to be *tāraka* (the saving) and the latter to be *amanaska* (mindless).
Thus:

the accomplishment of the yoga of the stars (*tārakayoga-siddhi*) occurs when the reflection of the moon and sun appears within the two pupils of the eyes. By means of the two stars, one perceives the solar and lunar disks; having ascertained that there exists a pair of solar and lunar disks in the space situated at the center of the head within the microcosmic egg (*piṇḍāṇḍa*), just like [the disks] in the macrocosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), one sees them through the two stars. Here too—

One should meditate upon [the Self] as joined with the mind by means of the vision of the identity of both; for in the absence of that union, there is no opportunity for the activity of the senses. Therefore, through inward vision, the Savior (Tāraka) alone is to be contemplated. || 9 ||

Having ascertained that the sun and moon exist within the microcosm (piṇḍāṇḍa) just as they do in the macrocosm (brahmāṇḍa), he states that the perfection of the yoga of the stars arises from seeing their identity with those [celestial bodies] by means of the stars: "The eyes... and so forth. The meaning is that just as a non-yogi perceives the sun and moon situated in the macrocosm through the stars aided by the mind, so too the yogi should behold the pair of sun and moon shining in the space above his own head through the stars aided by the mind. To the objection—"Since the perception of form depends upon the eyes, what is the use of the mind?"—he replies: "That... The sense is that when the mind is occupied elsewhere, the eyes and other senses lack the power to grasp forms and such; for there are scriptural texts such as, "I was elsewhere, therefore I did not see," and "My mind was elsewhere, therefore I did not hear. Since this is so, [therefore... || 9 ||
It should be understood as being of two kinds, distinguished by the manifest and the unmanifest.

That *tāraka* (the saving star) is of two kinds: the embodied (*mūrtitāraka*) and the formless (*amūrtitāraka*). That which ends at the senses is the embodied; that which transcends the pair of eyebrows is the formless. In all internal discernment of objects, practice joined with the mind is required. Because one perceives the Reality situated above those two stars through an inner vision joined with the mind, it is indeed Brahman, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*). Therefore, it is established that Brahman consists of pure white light. That Brahman is to be known by the inner vision of the eye aided by the mind. The same applies to the embodied *tāraka*. By the very eye joined with the mind, the "small space" (*dahara*) and so forth are to be known; for the purpose of perceiving form depends upon the mind and the eye, since the effect of perceiving form arises even internally through the conjunction of the self, the mind, and the eye, just as in the external world. Therefore, the inner vision joined with the mind serves to illuminate the *tāraka*. || 10 ||

(7) Regarding the question of how many kinds of things are to be contemplated, the answer is: "That which is the Star" (*tattārakam*). Just as the discernment of external objects depends upon the eye, so too the discernment of internal objects depends upon the mind and the eye; thus he says: "Everywhere. This is because of the vision of the Being situated above that [star]; that is, by perceiving the target of the superior star shining above the midpoint between the eyebrows. By what means is this to be seen? He says: "By that joined with the mind. It should be understood that Brahman alone is the target of the superior star. Because it is so, therefore: although the white light shining in the region of the midpoint between the eyebrows and elsewhere is a mental construction, since Brahman is all-pervasive, it exists there as well. Through the firm conviction that "this very [light] is Brahman," when the mind has dissolved therein, and in the absence of conceptualization—which requires a conceptualizer—Brahman alone remains free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*); this is the meaning. That light which was mentally constructed is Brahman. Because it is so, therefore. (10)

The nature of *tārakayoga*: when the gaze is fixed through the aperture between the two eyebrows upon the light manifested above that point, it becomes *tārakayoga*. Having properly joined the mind with that *tāraka* (the star-like light), one should, with effort and attentiveness, slightly raise the pair of eyebrows upward. This is the former *tārakayoga*. The latter, however, is called "formless" (*amūrtimat*) and "mindless" (*amanaska*). A great shaft of light exists in the upper portion at the base of the palate; that is to be meditated upon by yogis. From that, the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) such as *aṇimā* arise. || 11 ||

Regarding the question "What is this Tāraka-yoga?", the meaning is as follows: having fixed the pair of eyes upon the Ājñā-cakra located within the hollow space between the two eyebrows, one should meditate with full attention; that light which is to be contemplated by yogis is Brahman. As for what happens thereafter, it is stated: "From that... (verse 11).

The Śāmbhavī Mudrā occurs when the gaze, free from blinking or opening, is fixed upon the internal and external object of focus; through the dwelling of the knower who has ascended to that mudrā, the ground becomes pure. By his vision, all worlds become pure. Whoever receives the worship of such a supreme yogi also becomes liberated. || 12 ||
He states that what has been described by the yogis as the object of meditation culminates in the Śāmbhavī Mudrā itself: "Within... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "this becomes the Mudrā":
"The internal object of focus, while the gaze is directed outward, free from blinking or opening—the this is that Śāmbhavī Mudrā, hidden in all Tantras."

Thus says the Śruti. He praises the yogin who has ascended that mudrā with the words "That" (tad). Regarding the phrase "it becomes pure," it is because of the statement describing his own nature: "Purifying the surface of the earth by the mere placement of his feet. All those who move in the sky and those who move on the earth become pure when they come within the range of the vision of one who knows Brahman;
they are immediately liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million births.
Thus says the Śruti. || 12 ||
The internal object of focus (*antarlakṣya*) consists of various conceptualizations;

its essential nature is the blazing light within the internal object. By the instruction of the supreme guru, the internal object of focus becomes either the blazing light of the thousand-petalled lotus (*sahasrāra*), or the light of consciousness (*cijjyotis*) situated in the cave of the intellect (*buddhiguhā*), or the fourth consciousness (*turiyacaitanya*) abiding at the end of the sixteen. The vision of that [light] has the true teacher as its root. || 13 ||

Having conceptualized the internal object of focus, he determines it as "supreme. Since the aforementioned conceptualizations converge upon a single reality, he asks what the root of that vision is; to this, he replies: "that vision" (taddarśana). || 13 ||

The characteristics of the teacher: The teacher is one perfected in the Vedas, a devotee of Viṣṇu, free from envy, a knower of yoga, established in yoga, always having yoga as his very self, and pure. (14)
Endowed with devotion to the guru, and particularly possessing knowledge of men—one who is thus perfected in these characteristics is called a "guru. (15)
The syllable *gu* signifies darkness, and the syllable *ru* signifies its obstruction;
because it obstructs darkness, it is called *guru*. (16)
The Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman; the Guru alone is the supreme goal;
the Guru alone is the supreme knowledge; the Guru alone is the ultimate refuge. || 17 ||
The Guru alone is the supreme goal; the Guru alone is the supreme wealth.
Since he is the one who instructs in that [truth], the Guru is even greater than the Guru. 18.
Thus, having stated the definition of an Ācārya, he explains the meaning of the word *guru*: "The syllable *gu*," etc. (14–18).
The fruit of the study of this book:

for one who recites it even once, there is liberation from saṃsāra; all sin committed throughout all births perishes at that very moment; one attains all desires; and the accomplishment of all human goals occurs. For one who knows thus—this is the Upaniṣad. 19.

He states the fruit of reading and reflecting upon this text and its meaning with the word "yaḥ" (he who). For those with minds either full of desire or free from desire, the fruit of reading is the attainment of all desires and the attainment of the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha). Thus, the word "Upaniṣad" signifies the completion of the Advayatārakopaniṣad. || 19 ||
By Upaniṣadbrahmayogin, disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra,
this commentary on the Advaya Upaniṣad has been written, which has the Supreme Lord as its object.
It is said that the length of this commentary on the Advaya Upaniṣad is eighty [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Advayatārakopaniṣad, constituting the fifty-third [treatise] in the exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the ŚrīmadĪśa;
Oṃ, may this be offered to the venerable Ramacandra, the supreme guru and the Great Swan (Paramahaṃsa) who is the foundational substratum of the entire universe.
